n: The last chapter is a communal prayer. It has 22 verses like the Hebrew alphabet but is not an acrostic. It begins by asking the Lord to remember and look at his people’s disgrace.
The land God gave Israel as an inheritance now belongs to foreigners. Losing the land felt like losing the covenant promise itself.

f.g: The promised land, divided among the tribes as a permanent family inheritance.

n: Like orphans and widows—the most vulnerable people in ancient society—they have no protector.
They must now buy the water and firewood that once were freely theirs—everyday necessities under foreign control.

f.w: We have drunken our water for money

n: Pursuers are at their necks; they are worked hard and never allowed rest.

f.w: we labour, and have no rest

n: “Giving the hand” means making a treaty. Israel had turned to Egypt and Assyria for food and security rather than to God.

f.g: Pledged submission or made an alliance.

n: Our ancestors sinned and are gone, yet we bear the consequences. Ezekiel 18 will add that each generation also answers for its own choices.

f.w: Our fathers have sinned, and are not

n: Former slaves—officials of a foreign empire—now rule over them, and no one can rescue them.
Getting food meant risking one’s life because raiders roamed the countryside.
Starvation fever has scorched their skin as if burned in an oven.

f.g: Hot and blackened, as from fever and famine.

n: Women in Jerusalem and the towns of Judah were violated by the conquerors—one of the cruel realities of ancient war.
Princes were executed and hung up for display, and the elders received no respect.

f.g: Either hanged by the enemy’s hand or hung up by their own hands as a public humiliation.

n: Young men were forced to grind grain like slaves, and boys staggered under loads of wood.

f.g: Grinding grain at the mill was the work of slaves and captives.

n: Elders no longer sit at the city gate to judge, and young men no longer play music. Normal community life has stopped.

f.g: The city gate, where elders held court and public business took place.

n: Joy is gone; dancing has turned to mourning—the reverse of Psalm 30’s praise.

f.w: our dance is turned into mourning

n: “The crown is fallen”—their honor and kingship are gone. The people take ownership: “Woe unto us, that we have sinned!”

f.w: The crown is fallen from our head

n: Because of all this their hearts are sick and their eyes are dim with tears.
Mount Zion, the holy hill of the temple, now lies so empty that jackals roam over it.
The great statement of faith in the prayer: though the temple lies in ruins, the Lord still reigns forever. God’s throne was never in Jerusalem alone.

f.w: Thou, O LORD, remainest for ever

n: An honest question: why have you forgotten us for so long? Faith can ask hard questions of God.

The key prayer of the book: “Turn us to you, O Lord, and we shall be turned.” They ask God to begin the change in their hearts. Jewish readers repeat this verse after reading verse 22 so the book ends on hope.

f.w: Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned
renew our days as of old

n: The book ends with an unresolved question: “Unless you have completely rejected us and are very angry with us.” The answer comes elsewhere in scripture: God promised to gather and restore Israel.

f.w: But thou hast utterly rejected us
f.g: Often translated “unless you have utterly rejected us”—a fearful question rather than a final statement.
